The Tasmanian nativehen (Tribonyx mortierii) exhibits a relatively high basal metabolic rate for a member of the Rallidae, with respirometry trials revealing a maximum oxygen consumption of 573.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 573.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a core body temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This elevated metabolic demand is consistent with the species' active, terrestrial foraging lifestyle and its adaptation to the cool, temperate climate of Tasmania. Field studies indicate that this metabolic rate is maintained across much of the bird's active daily period, supporting the energetic costs of both locomotion and thermoregulation in an environment where ambient temperatures frequently fall well below this thermoneutral zone. The high metabolic throughput is also reflected in the species' rapid growth rates during the nestling phase, as chicks must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to fledge within a relatively brief developmental window. Comparative data from related gallinules suggest that the nativehen's metabolic intensity is among the highest recorded for the family, a trait that likely underpins its ability to exploit protein-rich invertebrate prey as a primary food source.

Eggs incubated under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] hatch after an average incubation period of 22 days [ab = 22 days], although natural clutches observed in the field show a broader range extending from 19 to 25 days depending on microclimatic variation within the nest. Newly emerged chicks have an initial wet body mass of approximately 45 grams [Ww0 = approximately 45 grams], a value that places them among the larger-bodied hatchlings within the Rallidae and reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated to each egg. This substantial initial mass confers a survival advantage during the first days of life, when chicks are entirely dependent on parental provisioning for both warmth and food. The incubation temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] represents an optimal thermal regime for embryonic development, balancing the rate of organogenesis against the energetic costs incurred by the incubating adult, which must maintain continuous contact with the clutch through the 22-day (22 days) [ab = 22 days] incubation period.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic period at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds. Sexual maturation occurs well after fledging, with puberty estimated at 126 days since birth [tp = 126 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. The time from hatching to fledging, by contrast, is considerably shorter; nestlings achieve sustained flight at 42 days since birth [tx = 42 days since birth] under this same thermal regime at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This approximately three-month span between fledging and the onset of gonadal activity allows juveniles to complete their somatic growth trajectory and develop the social behaviors necessary for successful territory acquisition. Adult body mass differs markedly between the sexes, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 1251 grams [Wwi = 1251 grams] while males attain a slightly larger ultimate wet weight of 1334 grams [Wwi = 1334 grams]. This moderate sexual size dimorphism aligns with the species' predominantly monogamous mating system, where males may experience selective pressure for larger body size during territorial contests over nesting sites.

First reproduction in the Tasmanian nativehen is deferred until approximately 1.9 years since birth [tR = approximately 1.9 years since birth], a delay that reflects the time required to secure a stable territory and achieve full adult body mass at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This age at first breeding is observed under field conditions where the birds maintain a core body temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] during their active metabolic periods. Females typically produce clutches containing 5 to 8 eggs [N_R_i = clutches containing 5 to 8 eggs], and may raise 1 to 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 1 to 2 clutches per year] during the extended spring and summer breeding season. This reproductive output is modest compared to many other gallinaceous birds, but the altricial nature of the chicks and the prolonged period of biparental care impose significant energetic constraints on the number of broods that can be successfully reared. The combination of moderate clutch size and limited annual breeding attempts suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward high offspring survival rather than maximizing fecundity.

Maximum lifespan in the wild for the Tasmanian nativehen is estimated at approximately 15.7 years [am = approximately 15.7 years] when measured under the 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] thermal conditions characteristic of the species' thermoneutral zone. This longevity is remarkably high for a bird of its body mass and is indicative of a slow-paced life-history strategy that emphasizes adult survival over high annual reproductive output. The species' extended lifespan is supported by its stable, resource-rich habitat and a relatively low predation pressure in its native range. Field records of banded individuals confirm that adults can maintain breeding territories for over a decade, with some individuals documented as still reproductively active beyond 12 years of age. This extended reproductive window partially compensates for the modest annual fecundity, allowing females to contribute multiple successful clutches over their long lifetimes.
